activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Chicago's Engine Company 21 is widely credited with the first fire pole, installed in 1878 after a firefighter slid down a pole faster than others could take the stairs.
story:
The visitor center at the Marsh Hollow Nature Reserve used to be Chicago's Engine Company 21, an old brick fire station with a symmetrical front and a square tower where the hoses once dried. Aiden noticed the brass pole first, running from the second floor straight down to the main room, polished bright and roped off with a velvet cord. "Who puts a slide in a fire station?" he asked.

"Nobody slides on it," said Priya, who had been reading the plaque by the door and clearly wanted to be the first one with the answer, because Ranger Dana had promised that whoever solved the pole riddle would get to release the rescued red-tailed hawk this afternoon. "It's for, like, decorations."

Ranger Dana gathered the class beside the pole. "Here's the riddle," she said. "Fire stations had these poles instead of just taking the stairs. Why? Take ten minutes, look around, and tell me your best guess. I'll only accept a full answer: the city, the year, and what actually happened." She handed out clipboards, because they were also supposed to sketch seeds that had begun to germinate in the greenhouse trays. Aiden could not have cared less about seeds right now.

He climbed the stairs to the second floor and counted: fourteen steps, a landing, then fourteen more. Then he stood at the top of the pole and stared down. The pole was one straight drop. The stairs zigzagged. He borrowed Maya's stopwatch and asked Marcus to time him doing stairs at a dead run: nine seconds, and he nearly flattened a display case of antique helmets doing it. Then he leaned over the pole and dropped his clipboard strap down it. It hit the floor in barely a breath. Straight down beat zigzag. That was the whole idea. The pole wasn't for fun; it was for speed. He found the date scratched into the brass collar at the base: 1878. Engine Company 21, Chicago, 1878. Somewhere back then, one firefighter had gone down the pole and beaten everybody else down the stairs, and after that, poles spread everywhere.

Priya got there first anyway, breathless, and said, "Because poles look cool and impress people!" Ranger Dana winced. "Partial diagnosis, but no." Aiden raised his hand and said, "Chicago's Engine Company 21 put in the first fire pole in 1878, after a firefighter slid down a pole faster than the others could take the stairs."

Ranger Dana unclipped the velvet cord, and a hour later Aiden stood in the open field behind the station with a leather glove on his arm and the hawk gripping it, wild-eyed and ready. "Go on," he whispered, and lifted his wrist toward the sky.

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons, so the atomic number also tells you how many electrons it has.
story:
Isabelle sat on an overturned bucket in her grandfather's garage, a poster of the periodic table spread across the workbench between a jar of screws and a coffee can full of pencils. Tomorrow she had to draw a model of a sodium atom for science, and she had exactly one clue: sodium's box said 11.

"Eleven what?" she asked the garage. The place smelled like motor oil and sawdust, and somewhere behind the lawnmower a cricket chirped, indifferent to her problem.

She ran her finger down the poster. Every box had a name, a symbol like Na, and a whole number in the top corner. Hydrogen had 1, helium had 2, carbon had 6. The numbers climbed as she moved across the rows. At the bottom of the poster, in small print, it said atomic number. That was the term, but it didn't tell her what to do with it. Her grandfather had left a chemistry book on the bench too, its cover soft from years of hands, and she flipped through it until she found a page about atoms. Protons, it said, live in the nucleus, and the atomic number is how many protons an element has. Sodium, then, had eleven protons. That part was solved, and it felt like finding the right wrench on the first try.

But her model needed electrons too, little dots to circle the nucleus, and the book page just showed a diagram without counting them. Isabelle chewed the end of a pencil. The atom in the picture was labeled neutral, which she'd heard meant balanced, like a battery with no charge. If the atom wasn't charged, she reasoned, the negative electrons had to cancel the positive protons exactly. So however many protons there were, there had to be the same number of electrons. She tested the idea with the diagram: it showed boron, atomic number 5, and when she counted the electron dots, there were five. She flipped to another diagram, oxygen, number 8, and counted eight electrons. Her rule held twice. It felt too simple to trust, but there it was, printed in the book over and over.

"So sodium gets eleven electrons," she said out loud. She sketched fast, a small nucleus labeled 11p and three rings around it, dots marching along each circle like a tiny tsunami of pencil marks sweeping around the nucleus. Some dots she'd have to squeeze together, which would make her drawing a temporary mess until she spaced them evenly, but she could fix that with the compass from the coffee can.

The garage door rattled up and her grandfather leaned in, sawdust on his sleeves. "Still at it, scientist?"

"Eleven protons, eleven electrons," she said, and held up the poster so he could see her pencil line drawn from sodium's box to her drawing. "The number does both jobs."

He squinted at the model, then tapped the nucleus twice with one thick finger. "Then label it, so tomorrow your teacher knows you figured that out on purpose."

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: On a distance-time graph, a steeper line means a faster speed.
story:
Jaxon's science teacher had assigned a rolling ball and a stopwatch, but the real reason he was taping a meter stick to the hallway floor was his little sister, Nina. She had left a note on his desk that morning: "You always say I cheat. Prove it with your science. Race me and make it fair." So he would. He had graph paper, a pencil, and a plan he hoped would conceal nothing from anybody.

He marked the floor every half meter from the wall to the bedroom door. The rules he wrote back to Nina were simple: each of them would roll a ball down the hall, he would time it, and they would draw both rolls on one distance-time graph. "Same hallway, same clock," he said when she came home. "That makes it impartial."

Nina rolled first. Jaxon clicked the stopwatch, called out the distance at each second, and wrote the numbers down. Her ball reached three meters in two seconds. Then he rolled his own, slower, and she did the calling while he wrote. When they plotted the points, two lines climbed the page from the bottom left corner.

"Yours is steeper," Nina said, leaning over the graph. "What does that mean?"

"Steeper line, faster speed," Jaxon said. "That's how it works."

Nina frowned. "But I won. Mine got to the door first."

"You rolled first. That's not the same thing." He tapped her line with the pencil. "Look where each line is at two seconds. Yours is higher. Your ball covered more ground in the same time, so you're faster. If we'd raced side by side, you'd have beaten me."

Nina read the graph again, tracing her line with one finger, then his. "So it doesn't matter that you wrote the numbers for my roll. The graph shows it anyway."

"That's the whole point," Jaxon said. "The clock doesn't take sides."

She grabbed a fresh ball from the toy bin. "Again. I want a steeper line than last time."

They rolled five more times, and on the fifth try her line leaned so far toward the top corner that Jaxon had to add distance to his graph. Nina stood over the paper, arms crossed, chin up, queen of the hallway. Jaxon's stomach had been in knots all afternoon waiting for her to cheat and ruin it, but everything had come out clean and the graph proved it to both of them.

That night he found a new note under his door. "Tomorrow can we do the ramp in the garage? I want to see if a ball going downhill makes a line that goes straight up. Also you're not as slow as the graph says. You just roll like your intestine is twisted." Jaxon laughed, taped the graph above his desk, and set the stopwatch on his pillow so he wouldn't forget it in the morning.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: Masaccio's Holy Trinity fresco in Florence, painted around 1427, is one of the earliest paintings built on a single vanishing point.
story:
Joseph had until four o'clock tomorrow to hang a drawing in the camp art show, and all he had was a lopsided street that looked like it had melted. The art cabin smelled of pine sap and pencil shavings, and rain ticked against the window while he stared at his page. His cabin had voted him into the show as a joke, mostly, and now the joke had a deadline.

"You're drawing it flat," said Priya, leaning over from the next stool. "Everything's the same size whether it's near or far."

"I know it's wrong. I just don't know what the rule is." He flattened the paper with his palm. "There has to be a rule. Roads don't get smaller for fun."

Priya dug through the supply shelf and came back with a print she'd won at the trivia night the counselors had held last week. "Look at this one. It's old." She set it beside his drawing. It showed a tall arched church interior with a figure on either side, painted in faded pink and gray.

"That's the Holy Trinity fresco," Priya said. "It's in a church in Florence. My cousin saw it. It was painted around 1427." She ran her finger along the ceiling lines. "Watch." Her fingertip traveled down the arch, down the column edges, down the pattern on the floor, and every time her finger stopped at the same spot, a point just above the altar, at the foot of the cross. She did it again with the coffered ceiling, and again the line landed there.

Joseph grabbed a ruler and laid it against the print's ceiling edge. He drew a light pencil line extending it on the protective sleeve. Then he did the floor lines, then the column. Six lines, all crossing at one point, like spokes on a wheel. "Everything runs to one spot," he said slowly. "If the lines all meet there, then stuff closer to it has to look smaller. That's the whole trick. It's not a feeling, it's math." He checked the edges again to be sure, and the seventh line hit the mark too.

"So maybe it's one of the first paintings ever built that way, on a single vanishing point like that," Priya said. "Somebody had to figure it out the same as you just did."

Joseph laughed. "It took me a ruler and a cheat sheet." He pinned a fresh sheet, marked a dot halfway across the page, and named it quietly. Then he fanned his pencil lines out from it like sunrays and drew his street along two of them, store windows shrinking as they ran inward. When his hand wavered, it felt like a small rebellion against the ruler, and the lamppost he drew freehand came out crooked, so he erased it and used the ruler after all.

By the time the counselor came through to install the show boards on the porch, Joseph had a finished street, with a bicycle leaning against a near doorway drawn large and a distant doorway drawn small. Priya held it up and tilted her head. "It looks like you could walk down it."

"Only if you walk toward that point," Joseph said, and tapped the dot with his pencil.

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: Keith Johnstone's 1979 book 'Impro' taught that characters in a scene play higher or lower status, and shifting status creates drama.
story:
Sarah's living room had been turned into a stage, which meant the coffee table was shoved perpendicular against the wall and two kitchen chairs sat in the middle of the rug. Her scene partner, Marcus from down the street, slumped in one chair, script-less and nervous.

"We're supposed to say yes, and to everything," Sarah reminded him. "That's the whole assignment. Ms. Ferreira said if you block somebody's offer, the scene dies right there."

"What if their offer is terrible?"

"Then you say yes, and it's terrible, and you build on it anyway."

They tried a scene. Sarah started as a librarian, and Marcus played a kid asking for a book on volcanoes. It was fine and it was flat, and they both knew it. After three minutes Sarah called, "Scene," and dropped onto the couch.

"My brother has a book that might help," she said. "He took improv in college." She dug through the box under the stairs and came back with a battered paperback, Impro, by Keith Johnstone, published in 1979. "He highlighted the whole thing. Look, he wrote 'status' next to this page about a hundred times."

She read while Marcus peeked over her shoulder. The pages said that characters in a scene play higher or lower status, and that shifting status creates drama. Sarah remembered her brother demonstrating it once in this same room, two years ago. He had played a king, all chin and slow blinking, ordering their cousin around as a servant, and the scene had crawled along until the cousin suddenly straightened up and started giving orders right back, telling the king to fetch tea and dry his muddy boots. The whole family had laughed until their sides hurt. Sarah hadn't known why it worked until this moment.

"Okay," she said, standing. "You be the king. I'm the servant. And halfway through, we flip."

Marcus gripped his imaginary crown. "Servant! Polish the royal boots."

"Yes, and then I'll press your royal trousers, Your Majesty," Sarah said, bending low, wiping an invisible boot with her sleeve. She shuffled backward, head down. "Is there anything else, my lord?"

"No. Wait. Yes. Fan me."

Sarah fanned him with a serving tray, then slowly stopped shuffling. She straightened her spine. "Actually, Your Majesty, I've been thinking. Your boots are my boots now. Fetch my slippers."

Marcus gaped for half a second, then dropped to one knee. "Yes, and I'll fan you as well, Your Majesty."

The scene accelerated from there, each of them climbing and falling, the servant ordering the king to juggle, the king meekly asking permission to sit on his own throne. When Sarah finally called "Scene," they were both laughing too hard to stand up straight.

Marcus pointed at the old paperback on the couch. "Can we use that trick for our grade?"

"That's not a trick," Sarah said, handing him a glass of water because his voice had gone scratchy. "It's the principle the whole thing runs on. Now go put the coffee table back before my mom sees."

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 9 to 12 hours of sleep a night for children aged 6 to 12 and 8 to 10 hours for teenagers aged 13 to 18.
story:
The waiting room wall was almost barren, just a faded poster about hand washing and a clock that ticked too loudly, so Clara pulled out her notebook and reread her list. For two weeks she had written down when her stomach knotted, when her hands went cold, when her head ached: Monday morning before the math quiz, Wednesday before she had to read aloud, every evening around nine. She was looking for a pattern, something hidden she could not see directly but might still catch on paper, the way you figure out a rule by watching what happens over and over.

"Clara," the nurse called, and Clara's mother followed her into a small room where Dr. Okafor weighed her, checked her ears, and then sat flipping through the pages Clara handed over. "Interesting," the doctor said. "You like evidence." Clara said she wanted to know what was causing the headaches, because if it was stress, she could learn to fight it, and if it was something else, all the fighting in the world would not oppose the real cause. Dr. Okafor asked what time she went to bed and what time she woke up. Midnight and six thirty, Clara admitted, because she texted with her cousin after her parents thought she was asleep. Her mother made a small sound in the corner.

"Kids your age need nine to twelve hours," Dr. Okafor said. "Teenagers, thirteen to eighteen, need eight to ten." Clara did the math on the back page of her notebook. Six and a half hours. Less than the bottom of the range, every single night. Dr. Okafor also showed her a breathing exercise: in for four, hold for four, out for six, ten rounds. "Try the sleep first," she said. "Test it like your notebook. One week."

That night Clara set her phone to charge in the kitchen, which felt like a punishment, and got into bed at nine. In the dark she did ten rounds of the slow breathing, and she noticed her shoulders drop somewhere around round six. She kept a tally on a sticky note on her mirror: hours slept, headaches, knots in her stomach. Thursday morning, day four, she woke before her alarm and realized she could not remember the last headache. Maybe the breathing helped, maybe the sleep did, maybe both, and she could not yet untangle which, which bothered her the way an unsolved problem always did.

On Friday her cousin texted at eleven: You up? Clara sat on the edge of her bed with the phone glowing in her hands, nine hours already banked if she fell asleep right now, and the old pattern pulling at her from the other side of the screen. She typed maybe and stopped. Her thumb hovered over send.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A percentage based on very few attempts can be misleading: a player who makes one shot out of one attempt shoots 100 percent.
story:
The phone buzzed against Antoine's math homework at 7:42 on Tuesday night. In the group chat, Dominique had posted a screenshot of the rec league stats page with the caption, "Guess who's the best shooter on the team." Her name sat at the top of the list at 100 percent. Antoine squinted at the tiny numbers beside it: one for one.

He remembered the game it came from, back in November, when Dominique had grabbed a loose ball near the free-throw line and tossed up a lucky shot at the buzzer. The gym had gone wild, and Coach had even let her elaborate on the play at the next practice, describing how she'd "seen the whole court." Antoine had been on the bench with a sprained wrist, watching from the sideline with a bag of ice taped on. One shot, he thought. One shot all season, and it went in.

Down the chat, Kayla, who took most of the team's shots, was getting annoyed. "I make nine out of twenty every game," she typed, "and I'm ranked below her?" Someone else wrote, "Stats don't lie." Antoine didn't answer right away. He opened the league page himself and started counting. Kayla's line said 45 percent. He did the math on paper: she had taken eighty shots and made thirty-six. Dominique had taken one and made one. A perfect percentage built on a single attempt. It felt naive to trust the number without looking at how many tries were behind it.

He typed carefully, because he didn't want to ruin Dominique's fun, only make the ranking fair. "One for one is 100 percent, but it's one shot," he wrote. "Kayla's is out of eighty. Shouldn't the list count how many attempts too?" Then he added, "Also whoever runs that site should know the ball covers are polymer anyway, so they clearly like numbers and materials, they can handle one more column." Kayla sent a row of laughing emojis. Dominique typed three dots, then stopped, then typed again. "Okay that's fair," she said. "Ask the league to add attempts."

Antoine emailed the league office that night, and by Thursday the stats page had a new column. Dominique was no longer first, but she didn't seem upset; at Friday's practice she told Kayla, "Feed me the ball, I'm due for shot number two."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Indonesia and Malaysia, the right hand is customarily used for eating and for giving or receiving things, as a sign of respect.
story:
Olivia had been trying for two weeks to figure out why Nadia's grandmother never took anything from her with a smile. Every time Olivia handed back a pencil or passed a worksheet, the old woman, who helped in the school office, would accept it with a stiff nod and turn away. At first Olivia thought the grandmother disliked her. But she watched carefully, and the pattern was strange: with other students she laughed and joked, and with Olivia, nothing.

She made a list in her notebook, feeling a bit eccentric sitting in the hallway writing down handshakes and nods like a detective. Greetings, she noticed, were part of it. When Mr. Peters welcomed the grandmother each morning, she pressed her palm to her chest and gave a small bow. When students waved, she waved back warmly. The problem had to be something Olivia herself was doing. She just couldn't see it.

Then Nadia invited her to dinner. "My grandmother insists," Nadia said. "She wants to repay the girl who found her reading glasses." Olivia had found them under the copying machine, so she couldn't very well postpone the invitation, even though she was nervous.

The table was crowded with dishes, and everyone waited until the grandmother lifted her spoon. Olivia watched, because watching was what she did now. Nadia's little brother reached for the rice with his left hand, and Nadia's father caught his wrist and gently moved it to his lap. "Right hand, Adi," he murmured. Every single person at the table ate with the right hand only. When Nadia passed the spiced beef, she used her right. When her mother offered the tea, right hand again. Olivia tested a small idea. She passed the cucumber salad across the table with her right hand, and Nadia's grandmother met her eyes and smiled for the first time all evening.

So that was it. All those stiff nods in the office. Olivia had been handing things over with her left hand every single day, because her right hand was usually holding her binder. In Indonesia and Malaysia, Nadia explained later, washing dishes at the sink, people customarily used the right hand for eating and for giving and receiving things. "It's a sign of respect," Nadia said, handing Olivia a towel with her right hand, and grinning. "Took you long enough. Grandma thought you were angry at her."

The next morning Olivia stopped by the office with a box of dates, a thank-you gift for the dinner. She held it out in her right hand and waited. The grandmother looked at the box, then at Olivia's hand, then at her face, and something changed in her expression, like a door unlocking. "You come Sunday," the grandmother said, in a voice that made it not a question. "There is someone I want you to meet."

activity: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
knowledge_domain: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
fact: An external stylesheet is connected to a web page by a link tag with rel="stylesheet" placed inside the page's head section.
story:
Marcus's basement smelled like lizard, which made sense because twelve tanks of them lined the wall, and because Marcus's bearded dragon, Rex, was currently demolishing a cricket on the carpet. "He's a carnivore," Marcus said, scooping the cricket legs into his hand. "Anyway. Can you make my site or not?"

That was the problem. Marcus wanted a bearded dragon fan page, one so good it might become influential in the reptile world, whatever that meant. Tyler wanted to be the one who built it. He had promised. He had exactly one afternoon.

He opened his laptop on the ping-pong table and started typing. He wrote the page in HTML: a big heading that said REX THE BEARDIE, a paragraph, a picture. Then he made a separate file called style.css and wrote the rule to centre the heading, checked the spelling twice, and saved everything. His heart was doing a small drumroll. This was the moment.

He refreshed the browser. The heading sat stubbornly on the left.

"No," Tyler said. He centred it again, more carefully this time. Refresh. Left. He checked for a missing semicolon, a typo, a stray capital letter. Nothing. The CSS file sat in the same folder as the page, plain as anything, and it might as well have been in another country.

"Looks fine to me," Marcus said, leaning over his shoulder. "Rex's eyes do that when he's about to bite somebody."

Tyler stared at the two files side by side. The page and the stylesheet were like two people in the same room who had never been introduced. Maybe the page didn't even know the stylesheet existed. He scrolled up to the top of his HTML, to the head section, where the title lived. If something connected the two files, that was where it would go. He typed a link tag, and inside it, rel="stylesheet" and the file name. He saved and refreshed, his finger hovering over the keyboard.

The heading slid to the exact centre of the screen.

Marcus whooped so loudly that Rex puffed his beard out. "You did it! Post it, post it right now!" He grabbed the laptop and uploaded the page, then leaned back, glowing, waiting for the reptile world to notice him.

Nothing happened for a second. Then a comment appeared, the very first one, from a user named RexTheBeardie: "This site's design is mine. I centred my heading in 2019."

Marcus looked at his dragon, who was watching the screen with one fixed eye. "No," he said slowly. "I changed that password last week."

The comment box blinked: New reply from RexTheBeardie.

activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
knowledge_domain: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
fact: In the absorption method, rice cooks in a measured amount of water that it soaks up completely, so no water needs to be drained.
story:
Sadie had boiled pasta at home a hundred times, so when the rice in her pot started looking soupy, she grabbed the colander and swung it toward the sink. "Whoa, stop!" Marcus lunged across the counter and knocked her hand aside. "That's absorption method. You measured the water on purpose. The rice is going to drink all of it." Sadie stared at the pot. "Drink it? All of it?" She had never cooked anything that swallowed its own water instead of getting drained.

Marcus wanted this more than she did. His grandmother was coming to visit in three weeks, and he was determined to make her flatbread without burning it, like she did, so today he kept circling the griddle side of their station while Sadie handled the curry and rice. Mrs. Okafor had set the challenge: rice, curry, and flatbread, all finished within the same five minutes. "It's not probable that we pull this off," Marcus said, wiping flour off his elbow. "Everything cooks at a different speed." Sadie copied the timing chart off the whiteboard anyway. Flatbread took minutes, curry simmered for half an hour, rice sat in the middle.

She started the curry first, then measured two cups of water for the rice and set the lid on tight. While it sat there doing whatever invisible thing it was doing, she noticed something. Every time she lifted the lid, steam billowed out and the top of the rice looked dry and wrong. When she left it alone for ten straight minutes, she could hear a faint change in the pot, a softer, hungrier sound. She decided to test it. Lid on, hands off, timer only.

The curry began to smell like her aunt's kitchen, sweet coconut and hot chili, and Marcus dropped his first flatbread onto the griddle. It blistered and puffed and he actually cheered. "Don't get comfortable," Sadie warned. "We still have the rice." When her timer went off, she lifted the lid, expecting soup. Instead, steam rolled up and the grains stood separate and whole, and there was no water left anywhere in the pot. She tipped it gently over the sink, just to be sure. Not a drop. Marcus pointed at it and said, "See? Absorption method. It soaked up every bit."

He nudged her with his elbow. "Okay, I accuse you of being good at this." Sadie scooped rice onto three plates, ladled the curry over it, and slid the last flatbread off the griddle with ten seconds still on the clock. Marcus took a bite of his flatbread, closed his eyes, and whispered, "Grandma's going to cry."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: The PG-13 movie rating was introduced in the United States on July 1, 1984, as a step between PG and R.
story:
Penelope had laced her skates three times, and the date hadn't even started yet. Marcus was due at the rink at two o'clock, and it was 1:58, and her best friend Dana kept circling the rink's bench like a shark with a boombox. Dana wanted to be the one who picked the music for the public skate session, because the rink manager had promised her the DJ booth if she showed up ten Saturdays in a row. This was Saturday number ten.

"You're going to fall," Dana said. "It's practically hereditary. Your mom told me your whole family can't skate."

"That's not how that works," Penelope said. "Also, don't talk to my mom." She rolled onto the ice, wobbled, grabbed the wall, and decided the wall was her new best friend. Marcus arrived at 2:03, red-cheeked from the cold, holding two hot chocolates. That was a good sign. He spilled one on his shoe within a minute. Also, possibly, a good sign, because now they were even.

They skated badly together for an hour, and then Marcus said the thing that mattered. "After this, movie? That new vampire one is at the four o'clock."

"The vampire one is rated R," Penelope said. "We're thirteen."

"No, it's PG-13," Marcus said. "My cousin saw it. PG-13's been around forever anyway."

Penelope didn't argue on the spot. She skated a slow lap and thought. If PG-13 had been around forever, her parents would have mentioned it, and more importantly, the theater's website would have said. At the concession stand she asked to see the newspaper on the counter and checked the movie listings. The vampire movie was, in fact, R. Then she found the part of the article about the ratings system, small print near the theater ads, and read it twice. "The PG-13 rating was introduced in the United States on July 1, 1984, as a step between PG and R." So not forever. Newer than her parents' record player, older than her parents' minivan. She tested the idea out loud: "Okay, it's a step between PG and R, and it started July 1, 1984. But your vampire thing is still R, so it doesn't matter."

Marcus looked at the paper, then at his shoes, still stained with hot chocolate. "So what can we see?"

"There's a PG thing about penguins. My little brother says one penguin gets eaten by a seal. It will consume your entire afternoon and you'll cry."

"I won't cry."

"My dad cried."

Over the speakers, the music cut off, and Dana's voice came over the rink's PA system, shaky but unmistakable: "This one goes out to everybody who's ever grabbed the wall the whole session." The opening drums of the loudest song in Dana's collection pounded out, and half the rink screamed with joy while the manager sprinted toward the booth.

Marcus held out his hand. "Penguins at four?"

Penelope looked at his hand, then at the ice, then back. "Only if we make it one full lap without the wall."

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: Each operation has an inverse that undoes it: subtraction undoes addition, and division undoes multiplication.
story:
The rain trapped Dylan at Grandpa's house with a math worksheet due Monday, and the problems stared back at him like locked doors. x + 7 = 12. He scratched out 5, then 7, then wrote them both and crossed them out again. Grandpa was out in the garage, and the house was so quiet Dylan could hear the refrigerator hum, indifferent to his crisis.

He tried brute force. He guessed numbers and tested them until his eraser wore a gray hole in the paper. If x were 5, then 5 + 7 would be 12, so x was 5. Fine. But the next one was 3x = 15, and guessing felt like the wrong way to live. He ripped a corner off his worksheet, folded it into a paper airplane, and sailed it at the couch. It hit the armrest and dropped. Even his airplane was failing him.

When Grandpa came in smelling of motor oil, Dylan slid the worksheet under a magazine. Too late. Grandpa picked it up, read it, and set it down. "Bathroom scale in the hall," he said, and walked to the kitchen like the conversation was over.

Dylan followed him anyway. The old scale's needle sat at some number he couldn't see because Grandpa had thrown a towel over the display. "Stand on it," Grandpa said. Dylan did. The needle moved somewhere under the towel. "Now hold this." Grandpa handed him a ten-pound bag of flour. The needle moved again, still hidden. "How much do you weigh without the flour?"

"Take the bag off."

"There it is." Grandpa went back to his coffee.

Dylan stood on the scale holding the bag, then without it, and stared at x + 7 = 12 until the numbers stopped looking like a wall. Something sat on top of x, the way the flour sat on him. He could take it off. He wrote x + 7 - 7 = 12 - 7, and the left side slumped down to plain x. "Subtraction undoes addition," he said out loud, mostly to the scale.

The 3x = 15 problem came next, and he turned it over in his head. Three x's, pressed together. If taking away undoes adding, something had to undo multiplying. He wrote x = 15 ÷ 3 and got 5, checked it, and 3 times 5 really was 15. He classified both problems in his notebook margin with a triangle and a star, his own private system.

That night he texted his friend Marcus: "figured out the whole worksheet. i am basically a wizard now." Marcus replied with a picture of his dog wearing sunglasses and the words "still failed the quiz." Dylan laughed, then noticed the last problem on the sheet: 4x + 6 = 22. Two things sitting on x. He picked up his pencil.

"One at a time," he muttered, and started subtracting.

activity: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
knowledge_domain: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
fact: In a pick and roll, after setting the screen, the screener turns and moves toward the basket, ready for a pass from the ball handler.
story:
Jeremy got the note from Coach Ruiz's mailbox before fourth period, folded into a square the size of a gum wrapper. "Friday scrimmage. You're running point. I want to see plays called, not just passes thrown," it said, and that was all. Three days. He crumpled the note into his jacket pocket and spent math class sketching the half court in his notebook, drawing arrows that looped and crossed like plumbing under a sink, ugly but approximate, enough to show where the ball might go.

The problem showed up at Wednesday practice. He had the play, a pick and roll, and he had the screener, Marcus, who was built like a door. Jeremy waved the signal, two taps on his hip, and Marcus jogged out and planted himself beside the defender. Jeremy rubbed his man off the pick and curled past it, ball high, ready. Then he looked up and there was nothing to see. Marcus stood where he had set the screen, flat-footed, watching the ball like a spectator. Both defenders recovered, the passing lane closed, and Jeremy forced a shot that clanked off the back rim.

"Nobody was open," Marcus said when they jogged back.

"You were supposed to be open." Jeremy chewed on it through the water break. It wasn't that Marcus was lazy. It had to be something about the play itself, something he hadn't drawn right in his notebook. The screen worked, the defender got caught, so the opening had to exist somewhere. He kept turning it over while the second-stringers scrimmaged, and finally he pulled the crumpled note from his pocket and smoothed it against his knee. Coach wanted him calling plays. Fine. First he had to know what the play actually was.

He borrowed his older sister's basketball book that night and found the page. There it was in the diagram, an arrow he'd never drawn, the second arrow. After setting the screen, the screener turns and moves toward the basket, ready for a pass from the ball handler. It wasn't two separate actions, it was one continuous thing. Marcus didn't stand because he was lazy, he stood because neither of them knew the second half of the move.

Thursday, Jeremy got to the gym early and taped one of his notebook pages to the bleachers. "You don't stop," he told Marcus. "You set the pick, then you roll to the basket. That's the whole play, that's why it's called a pick and roll." Marcus squinted at the sketch. "So I'm moving the whole time?" "The whole time."

Friday, the scrimmage was rough in the first quarter, defenders sniffing out the hand taps, once stealing the ball clean. But with two minutes left and his team down one, Jeremy called it. Marcus thundered out, set the pick hard enough to make the defender stumble, and then, instead of standing, he pivoted and cut toward the hoop with his hands up. Jeremy whipped the pass between two defenders. Marcus laid it in off the glass, and the net barely moved. From the sideline, Coach Ruiz wrote something on her clipboard and did not call a timeout. "Same play," Jeremy shouted, backing up the floor. "One more time."

activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
knowledge_domain: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
fact: Proportional representation more often produces coalition governments, because a single party rarely wins more than half the votes.
story:
Sophie had been dreading the city hall workshop ever since her class signed up, because the flyer said "Mock Parliament" and she had no idea what any of it meant. Now she stood at a long table in a room with high ceilings, holding a card that said PURPLE PARTY, 34% of the vote. Across the table, Marcus held a card that said ORANGE PARTY, 30%, and Priya had GREEN PARTY, 22%. The instructor, a woman with a clipboard, had taped two big charts to the wall and told them to figure out who won.

"Easy," Marcus said, pointing at the first chart. "Under first-past-the-post, whoever wins the most districts forms the government. Purple won the most districts, so we win." Sophie scrutinized the chart, leaning close enough to smell the marker ink. The Purple Party had taken 55% of the districts with only 34% of the votes, because its supporters were packed into certain neighborhoods while Orange and Green voters were scattered everywhere. "That seems biased toward Purple," she said slowly. "They got a third of the votes but more than half the seats."

The instructor tapped the second chart and said only, "Now try it the other way. Seats match votes." Sophie did the math on the back of her handout. Purple got 34 seats out of 100, Orange got 30, Green got 22, and a small Blue Party got 14. She added them twice. Nobody had more than 50. "So who's the government?" she asked. "Nobody," Priya said. "Not yet."

The rule card on the table said a government needed more than half the seats, and the clock on the wall gave them ten minutes. Marcus immediately tried to boss everyone around, declaring Purple the winner again because it was the biggest. Sophie felt a twist of guilt for even considering it, but she pushed her chair back and said, "It doesn't work like that here. Nobody has a majority, so two of us have to team up." Priya grinned and slid her Green card across the table. "Green plus Orange is 52," she said. "That's a coalition." Marcus stared at his card, out of power for the first time all morning.

Then came the twist. Sophie and Priya started dividing up the cabinet positions, arguing about who got the Environment Ministry, when a quiet boy named Tomas cleared his throat. He had been holding the Blue Party card, the smallest one, and everyone had ignored him. "If you two can team up," he said, "so can we. Purple plus Blue is 48, and if Green betrays you, we'd only need..." He paused, redoing Sophie's math on his fingers. "We'd need you." Suddenly the smallest party at the table was being courted by everyone at once.

The instructor called time. "Congratulations," she said. "You've just discovered that proportional representation more often produces coalition governments, because a single party rarely wins more than half of the votes." Sophie looked at the chart, then at her handout, then at Priya's outstretched hand, and shook it. "Deal," she said. "But we get Environment."

activity: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
knowledge_domain: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
fact: Excel's 'Show Values As' option can display each count as a percentage of its column or row total, so grades with different numbers of students can be compared fairly.
story:
Brooke sat cross-legged on the living room rug with her mom's laptop balanced on a cushion, because the school tech club had put her in charge of the survey results and she had promised her friends a real answer by Friday. The survey asked which lunch special students liked best, and 187 kids from four grades had answered. Her problem was that she had no idea how to make sense of a spreadsheet with 187 rows in it, so she had spent the evening watching tutorial videos and building her first pivot table while her dad watched TV above her head.

The pivot table itself felt like magic at first. She dragged Grade into the rows, dragged Lunch Choice into the columns, and dropped Count into the values, and the whole mess of rows collapsed into a tidy little grid. Then she read the numbers and felt her stomach drop. The pizza column was enormous. Pizza won in every single grade, and it wasn't even close.

"That can't be right," she muttered. "Half my grade picked the wraps."

Her dad lowered the volume. "So the survey's wrong?"

"No, I don't think so." Brooke chewed her pen and thought back to the morning she'd handed out the survey, when she'd given a form to every student in the eighth grade hallway but only found two sixth grade classes because the gym was flooded and the sixth graders were doing some assembly about plumbing repairs in the gym bathroom. That was it. There were way more eighth graders in her data than sixth graders, so of course the eighth grade's favorite, pizza, looked like a landslide. She couldn't see the imbalance directly in the count table, but she could deduce it from the row totals. Now she needed to test whether percentages would fix it.

She right-clicked a number in the grid and hunted through the menu until she found something promising: Show Values As. She picked the option that displayed each count as a percentage of its row total, so each grade's row added up to one hundred percent no matter how many students were in it. The grid shifted. Pizza still led in most grades, but the sixth grade row suddenly showed the wraps at fifty-two percent, winning outright, and the seventh grade race tightened to a near tie. Grades with different numbers of students could finally be compared fairly.

Her dad leaned over the back of the couch. "So what's the verdict?"

"Wraps win sixth grade, pizza wins seventh and eighth, and it's a tie in fifth," Brooke said. She thought about her first draft summary, the one she'd almost sent to the club that afternoon declaring pizza the champion, and was glad she hadn't. "Also, I was completely wrong an hour ago."

"Nice," her dad said. "Wrong is just the first draft of right."

Brooke saved the file and started typing her report. "Fifth grade, we need a rematch. Bring more people."

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: On a standard 400-metre outdoor track, the 800 metres is exactly two laps, so runners plan the race as a first lap and a second lap.
story:
The rink's indoor track circled the ice like a balcony, four laps to every kilometre, and Charlie had been running it all winter in borrowed skates' shadow while her brother practiced below. Now she had a letter in her jacket pocket, folded twice. It was from the regional meet director: her entry for the 800 metres was confirmed, outdoor track, first race of the season in eleven days. She read it again between intervals, the paper going soft at the creases.

Her problem showed up on the second interval. She sprinted the first lap, felt like a hero for about ninety seconds, and then died so completely in the second lap that a walker in a puffy coat passed her near the boards. "Same as last time," said Priya, leaning on the rail. "You spend everything early." Charlie thought about that on the bus home, turning the race over in her mind like a stone. The 800 wasn't one long effort; on a standard 400-metre outdoor track, it was exactly two laps, which meant the race had a shape, a first half and a second half, and she had been running it like a shapeless sprint.

The next practice she ran on the balcony track in halves, because two laps up there were equivalent to one lap outdoors. She timed each half and tried to regulate her breathing so the first felt controlled, almost easy, saving something she couldn't see or measure but could feel building in her legs like a debt held for later. When she pushed at the end, the speed was actually there. "Where were you hiding that?" Priya shouted. "In the first lap," Charlie called back. "I was hiding it in the first lap."

At the meet, the sun was on the white oval and the starter's gun cracked like ice splitting. Charlie held her plan through the first lap, ignoring the girl in lane three who surged far ahead. Near the end of that lap, the surge turned into a full kick, arms pumping, face tight, and Charlie felt a cold certainty: that girl thought it was the finish. It wasn't. The 800 was two laps, and she had one more to go. The girl crossed into the final lap first, then faded so badly she was swallowed by the pack before the backstretch.

Charlie finished fourth, which stung, because third got a medal and third was only half a stride away. She found the early kicker afterward, hands on knees by the fence. "I thought it was over," the girl said. "It's two laps," Charlie said. "I counted wrong all season." The girl nodded, and Charlie jogged toward the exit, where her brother waited with the folded letter in his hand, holding it out so she could read the last line again: her seed time had been beaten by four seconds. She put the letter in her pocket, next to the small hollow place where the medal would have gone, and they walked to the car without talking.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Pressing a trumpet valve sends air through an extra loop of tubing, making the air column longer and the note lower.
story:
Florence sat in the third row of the empty auditorium with her borrowed trumpet on her lap, staring at the three valves like they were keeping a secret from her. Seven notes she could get without pressing anything, but three little buttons made dozens. It didn't add up. Three buttons ought to make three notes, maybe four if you counted no buttons at all.

She had come in early before community band practice because her bedroom was too small for loud mistakes, and the auditorium swallowed them politely. She lifted the horn and played an open note, listening. Then she pressed the middle valve alone and blew. The note dropped, lower than before. She let it go, and the note climbed back up. She tried the first valve alone. Lower again, but by a different amount.

"So the buttons don't just pick notes," she said out loud, because the empty seats didn't mind. "They change the tubing." She slid the trumpet out of its case and turned it over in the light from the stage. The piping coiled and looped like a brass maze, and she followed one loop with her finger until she lost it behind another. She couldn't see inside, which was exactly the problem. Something invisible was doing all the work.

She tested it, one idea at a time. She hummed an open note, then pressed the second valve and hummed the note she'd heard. Pressing the valve made the note lower, every single time, never higher. Then she pressed all three at once, and the sound came out so low and wobbly that she laughed and the laugh turned into a squeak. The more tubing she used, the farther the sound slid down, as if the air had to walk a longer hallway before it was allowed out.

"Every valve opens an extra loop of tubing," she said to the trumpet. "So the air column gets longer, and the note gets lower." She tried combinations, writing them on her music folder: none, two, one, one and two. She was halfway through her list when footsteps echoed behind her, and Mr. Alvarez's nephew Theo, who played tuba, dropped into the seat beside her.

"That's my aunt's old horn," he said, leaning over. "The valve caps on the loops are sticking. Watch the third one." He pointed at a small cap on a coiled loop near the middle of the tubing, and when Florence pressed the third valve, she saw it: that cap barely moved, the loop only half engaged. That was why her three-valve notes had sounded sour all week. She polished the cap with her sleeve, spun it a quarter turn the way Theo mimed, and pressed the valve again. The note came out round and full and low.

Florence raised the trumpet and ran her new combinations up and down, one clean note after another, while Theo kept time on the armrest with his palm.

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: Hydrogen has atomic number 1, so every hydrogen atom has exactly one proton.
story:
Arthur had one goal at the science museum: beat the new exhibit before his sister Bea did. The exhibit was a giant touch-screen periodic table built into a wall shaped like a plateau of glowing squares, and a sign above it read, "Find the simplest element on the table. Win bragging rights."

"Simplest," Bea read out loud. "That's got to be gold, because it's the prettiest."

"That's not what simplest means," Arthur said, but he wasn't sure what it did mean. He started in the bottom rows, poking at squares. Uranium, number 92. Lead, 82. Everything down here had huge numbers in the corners, and the numbers felt like clues, though clues to what he couldn't say yet.

"Give up?" Bea teased after five minutes. "Want me to document your failure with a photo?"

"Push the wrong square again and I'll document yours." He worked his way up the wall, row by row, watching the numbers shrink: 20, then 11, then 6. It was like walking down a mountain, and the top of the mountain had to be the smallest number of all. He climbed to the top row and looked at the far left corner, and there it was, the very first square, sitting alone like a kid at the front of the class. Hydrogen. The number in its corner was 1.

"Every hydrogen atom has exactly one proton," the screen announced when he tapped it. "Atomic number 1 means one proton. That's what makes it the simplest element." Confetti exploded across the display, and Arthur did a small victory spin that he would later deny.

Bea peered at the square. "One proton? That's barely an atom. That's an atom with one sock."

"And it's still beating you." He tapped carbon next, number 6, and read its protons off the corner. Six. Then oxygen, 8. The rule held all the way down, and he began racing through squares, calling out numbers like a game show host.

A museum guide wandered past and smiled at the confetti. "You two found hydrogen, I see. First one today."

"Top left corner," Arthur said, pointing. "One proton. It was hiding in plain sight the whole time."

"Ironic," Bea said, "that the answer was the easiest thing to find, and we both made it hard." She grabbed his sleeve and dragged him toward the next room. "Come on, genius, the dinosaurs aren't going to defeat themselves."

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: The Sieve of Eratosthenes, an ancient Greek method, lists primes by crossing out the multiples of each prime in turn.
story:
Blake stared at the screen in Dev's basement, where the words "Enter a number:" blinked at him like a challenge. The program was supposed to say whether a number was prime, and it was supposed to say it correctly, which was the part currently failing.

"Nine is not prime," Dev said, reading the output. "Your program says it is."

"That's impossible. It only divides by two." Blake leaned closer to the laptop, as if the bug might crawl out where he could see it. Bugs were like that, he thought. You couldn't watch one work. You could only see the mess it left behind, like footprints in snow, and work backward.

"So follow the footprints," Dev said, sounding way too pleased with himself. He pulled a marker and a sheet of paper out of a drawer full of markers, paper, and one very old granola bar. "Write the numbers one to fifty. We'll check every answer by hand."

Blake copied the grid while Dev typed another test. "Twenty-five," Dev called. The program declared it prime. Five times five, Blake thought. Twenty-five was definitely not prime, so the program was wrong in a way it hadn't been wrong for nine, and the hidden cause had to be the same one, just hiding better.

"Your program's like a consumer that trusts the label and never checks the box," Dev said.

"It's not a consumer, it's obstinate," Blake said. "I told it to divide by everything up to the number, and it just... isn't." He squinted at the loop. There. The range stopped one step too early. He fixed it, ran it again, and twenty-five came back not prime. "Ha!"

"Now we check the whole grid," Dev said, and started crossing out numbers. He circled two, then crossed out four, six, eight, every second number. Then he circled three and crossed out its multiples in turn. Then five, then seven. What remained, uncrossed, were the primes.

"Wait," Blake said, scanning the paper. "Eleven, thirteen, seventeen. My program says those are prime too. Every single one matches."

"Know what this is called?" Dev said, holding up the paper. "The Sieve of Eratosthenes. Some ancient Greek method."

"So my laptop and a guy with no electricity agree," Blake said. "Two thousand years apart."

Dev grinned and slid the granola bar across the table in tribute. Blake pocketed it, typed "one hundred and seven" into the program, and the word "prime" popped onto the screen.

activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
knowledge_domain: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
fact: A soliloquy is a speech in which a character, usually alone on stage, speaks their private thoughts aloud so the audience can hear them.
story:
Claire slid Hamlet across the study table until the book stopped against the lamp, its edges worn soft by a hundred hands before hers. The assignment was due Monday: paraphrase Act Three, Scene One into modern English, and Mrs. Okafor had written one word in red at the top of the instruction sheet, "soliloquy," underlined twice. Claire was fairly sure she was the only one in ninth grade who didn't know what it meant, and she wasn't about to ask Devon, who had already told half the cafeteria that she'd spelled "rhythm" wrong on the last quiz.

The library hummed around her, quiet but not silent: the heater ticking, a cart of returns squeaking somewhere behind biography, the smell of old paper and lemon floor cleaner. She read the first line again. "To be, or not to be, that is the question." Easy enough. She wrote, "Should I keep living, or should I not." Then the speeches turned strange. Hamlet wasn't talking to anyone. No Horatio, no Ophelia, nobody. He just stood there spilling everything, thinking out loud about death and sleep and dreams, and the more she read, the more it felt like eavesdropping through a wall.

She flipped back through the scene, checking each speech. When Claudius spoke, Rosencrantz answered him. When Polonius lectured Ophelia, she at least stood there listening. But Hamlet's long speeches had no listener at all, and that was the pattern, the same shape repeating. She grabbed a pencil and drew a small X beside every speech where the character was alone, talking to nobody but the room. Four X marks. Then she flipped ahead to the scene where Claudius prays, and found another X there too, a king alone, confessing a murder to the empty air.

Her pencil went still. Claudius wasn't confessing to anyone in the play. He was confessing to her, to whoever sat in the dark beyond the stage. That was the trick of it, and she felt the whole structure click into place like a combination lock. The word itself must mean this, a private speech poured out on purpose so the audience hears the secret. She underlined "soliloquy" in her notebook and wrote beside it, "alone on stage, thoughts aloud, audience eavesdrops." Then she began the paraphrase again, slower this time, because now the words had a direction, like a letter addressed to her seat in the theater.

At the next table, Mr. Ferris from the front desk was reshelving parliament debates from the history section, thick blue volumes that smelled of dust. "How's the Bard treating you?" he asked, peering over.

"Better now," Claire said. "He's telling me secrets."

She read Hamlet's line once more, wanting her version to preserve that private, overheard feeling rather than flatten it. The heater ticked. Down the aisle, the book cart squeaked and stopped. She wrote, "The real question is whether to keep going at all, and whether it's braver to put up with everything or to end it," then crossed out "everything" and wrote "the whole mess," because that was how a boy alone at midnight would actually say it. Somewhere behind biography, a page turned, soft as a held breath.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Since 1996 the Internet Archive has been saving copies of public web pages, and its Wayback Machine lets anyone look at old versions of many websites.
story:
The food court smelled like fryer grease and cinnamon pretzels, and Oliver had exactly forty minutes before his mom picked him up. He set his tray down across from Priya, who was already scrolling on her phone. "I need your help," he said. "Last night my dad mentioned a blog he wrote before I was born, about his pizza shop. He thinks it's gone forever. I want to find it."

Priya locked her phone. "Websites die, Oliver. When a page gets deleted, where would it even go?"

"That's what I want to figure out." He pulled a napkin toward him and wrote the blog's old address from memory: pizzaoliver.blogspot. His dad had repeated it twice at dinner, laughing about the cheesy header photo. "If it's deleted, there's nothing to load. But something has to hold old pages somewhere, or nobody could ever prove what a site used to say." He had tried the address on the mall's free Wi-Fi kiosk already and gotten a dead link. So the next candidate had to be somewhere that kept copies, if such a place existed at all.

Priya leaned over the napkin. "Type the address into the Wayback Machine," she said. "It's this thing my brother uses to win arguments. He pulls up a store's website from ten years ago to show the price was lower." She typed it in, and a timeline appeared, dotted with little marks going back years. One mark sat all the way at the far end. She tapped it. The screen filled in with his dad's old blog, header photo and all, the whole page exactly as it had looked decades ago.

"Who keeps that?" Oliver asked, scrolling through posts about flour deliveries and a broken oven. The page even had a photo of the shop with the old sign, back when it was near the fountain, three stores down from where they were sitting. Priya shrugged. "Some place called the Internet Archive. It's been saving copies of public web pages since 1996. Anyone can look." Oliver read that line off the bottom of the screen, then looked up sharply. "Wait. Anyone. So if my dad posted a photo of the shop's old location, strangers can still see it. That means people can find out where a place was, years later, from stuff they thought was gone."

They tested it. Priya pulled up her own old dance-studio page in the archive and found a post from three years ago with the studio's address and a photo of her in the recital lobby, which she had completely forgotten publishing. She went quiet, then deleted nothing, because you couldn't delete it anyway; she just screenshotted it to show her mom. Oliver screenshotted his dad's blog too. Then he pocketed the phone, dumped their trays, and walked toward the fountain to find the spot where the old sign used to hang, holding the picture up next to the real wall. "Right there," he said. "Behind that toxic-green smoothie stand."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Sikhs celebrate Vaisakhi as the day in 1699 when Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur.
story:
The line for the langar hall stretched past the glass doors, and Maya could hear the dhol already thumping inside the cultural center. She had one job today, which was to keep her seven-year-old cousin Harjit from wandering off, and one wish, which was to trade jobs with anyone. Her older cousin Simran got to carry the orange flag at the front of the Vaisakhi procession this afternoon, and Maya envied her so much it made her jaw tight.

"Stay by me," she told Harjit, gripping his sleeve. Behind them, the parking lot was filling with cars and a small knot of geese traced overhead, the first of the migratory birds heading north, though nobody else seemed to notice but her.

"Maya, why is everyone so happy today?" Harjit asked. "Is it because of the food?"

She opened her mouth and realized she didn't have a good answer. It was a harvest thing, she thought. New year, spring, like the poster in the lobby with the wheat on it. "Something like that," she said, and hated saying it, because Harjit repeated everything and would announce her guess to the whole hall.

At the door, Uncle Kirpal was handing out small paper flags. Harjit tugged his kurta. "Uncle, why does this day matter?"

Uncle Kirpal smiled, but he was busy, and his answer came in pieces as he passed out flags. "Vaisakhi. The year 1699." He handed a flag to a boy. "Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru." Another flag. "He founded the Khalsa at Anandpur." Then he was swallowed by the crowd.

Maya stood still, holding the pieces together in her head like a puzzle she hadn't known was a puzzle. So it wasn't mainly the wheat. It was that. She bent down to Harjit's level, because if he was going to repeat her words all afternoon, they should be right ones. "It's about something that started a long time ago," she said. "In 1699, Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur. That's what we're celebrating."

Harjit nodded slowly, the way he did when he was filing something away. Then he raised his paper flag and marched toward the dhol, and Maya followed, her hand hovering an inch from his collar.

In the hall she found her mother arranging trays and made her offer, a quick negotiation: she would serve food for the whole afternoon if, next Vaisakhi, her name went on the list for the flag. Her mother squinted at her, then at Harjit, who was already telling a stranger, "1699," with enormous confidence.

"Deal," her mother said, and handed her a tray. "Start with that table by the window."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: A 2018 study by Jeffrey Hall of the University of Kansas found it takes about 50 hours together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend.
story:
Piper counted the seats before she counted the faces, because the desks told her something the people wouldn't. Twenty-six desks, twenty-five filled, one empty beside a girl with a green binder full of guitar tabs. She took it. The girl glanced over, then back at the board.

"You're new," the girl said when the teacher turned to write.

"Piper."

"Marisol."

That was all until lunch, when Marisol set her tray down across from Piper without asking. Piper had planned to eat alone and text her old friends in Millbrook, but the phone stayed in her pocket. They talked about the guitar tabs, then about a teacher who assigned homework on Fridays. Thirty-one minutes, Piper figured, maybe thirty-five with the walk to the table.

That night she looked up what she half remembered from a magazine in the dentist's office. There it was: a 2018 study by Jeffrey Hall of the University of Kansas found it takes about 50 hours together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend. She read it twice. Fifty hours. She did the math on the back of her science homework. Lunch was about half an hour. At one lunch a day, a hundred days, more than the whole school year. That couldn't be right for everybody. Her best friend Dana had taken a single disastrous summer of soccer camp to become inseparable, but that was hours a day, every day. It added up faster than Piper had ever thought about.

So she ran a test. She wrote 35 on a sticky note and stuck it inside her binder. Every lunch, every group project, every walk to the bus loop, she added the minutes. Thursday brought a surprise: Marisol sat with her at lunch and then again in study hall, and Piper caught her sneaking a look at the sticky note.

"What's the number for?"

"Hours. Sort of." Piper flattened the note on the desk. "There was this study, 2018, Jeffrey Hall, University of Kansas. It takes about fifty hours together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend. I'm keeping track."

Marisol frowned at it. "That's weird and also not wrong."

"You think it's wrong?"

"I think it's slow." She tapped the number. "My grandmother says friendship isn't an antibiotic, one dose and done. You have to take the whole course."

Piper laughed, the first real one in two weeks. "My mom says I inherited my stubbornness from my grandfather. The rebellious gene, she calls it."

"Good," Marisol said. "Then don't wait for the study to hit fifty." She pulled out her phone. "Saturday. My cousin's band plays at the community center. It's three hours and it's loud and you'll hate half of it."

Piper looked at the sticky note, then wrote +180 under the 35.

"Pick me up at six," she said.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Caramelization is browning that happens when sugar alone is heated, which makes it a different reaction from the Maillard reaction, which also needs amino acids.
story:
The Coleman stove hissed on the picnic table while Thomas poured a cup of sugar into the heavy pot his dad always called the dynasty pot, because it had survived three generations of family camping trips. Tonight it was his turn to make dessert, and he had decided on caramel, the real kind, made from nothing but sugar and heat.

His little sister Maya leaned over his shoulder as the sugar began to melt. "It's turning brown," she said. "Is that the same browning as the crust on the roast? Dad's roast got all brown this afternoon too."

Thomas stirred slowly and thought about it. The roast had browned in the fire, and the sugar was browning on the stove, but something felt different about the two. The roast was meat, and meat was not just one thing. The pot held sugar alone, nothing else. He remembered a page from a science book at the school library, something about browning reactions having names depending on what was in the pot.

"I don't think they're the same," he said. "The browning in this pot is called caramelization, because it happens when sugar alone is heated. The crust on the roast is a different reaction, the Maillard reaction, and that one also needs amino acids." Maya wrinkled her nose at the word, and he shrugged. "Meat has amino acids. Sugar doesn't. That's the difference."

"Prove it," Maya said, which was her favorite thing to say lately.

He couldn't exactly prove what was happening inside the pot, since browning was invisible work, molecules changing where no one could watch. But he could test the rule. He spooned a tiny pile of plain sugar onto a piece of foil and set it near the fire, then set a small piece of the roast beside it. Both browned, but he already knew that would happen, so it proved nothing. The real test was the other direction: he took a spoonful of his caramel, which contained no amino acids at all, and mixed a pinch of baking soda into part of it to see whether the browning would cease or keep going when he moved the pot off the heat. The color held. Sugar alone could do this. It didn't need anything from meat.

The caramel finished at exactly the right moment, amber and glossy, and Thomas poured it over sliced apples in the dented metal bowl. His dad came back from the wash station and took the first bite, his eyebrows going up in a way that made Maya laugh. "Endangered species, this dessert," Dad said, going back for seconds. "It won't survive the night." Thomas dished out the last of it before his sister could beat him to it.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: PolitiFact, a US fact-checking website founded in 2007, rates claims on a scale it calls the Truth-O-Meter, from True to Pants on Fire.
story:
The spaghetti steam fogged Hailey's glasses as Dad launched into the ad again. "It said half the town's water has poison in it. Half, Hailey. You're drinking it right now." He tapped her water glass with his fork, twice, like a tiny judge banging a gavel.

"That sounds off," Hailey said. She twirled noodles, listening to her little brother slurp beside her. "A commercial can say whatever it wants. That's not the same as it being true." Mom stirred her sauce and said ads were allowed to have opinions, the same way Grandma was allowed to think cats were better than dogs. Hailey put her fork down. "But a cat being better is an opinion. Nobody can look it up. Water having poison in it is different. Somebody could actually test that."

"So test it," Dad said, scooping more garlic bread. "Go ahead, refute the nice television."

She pulled out her phone, thumbs already moving. Grandma sniffed at phones at the table, but Grandma wasn't here tonight, and Dad had literally challenged her. She typed the exact words from the ad, the ones about water in a town. A result popped up fast, from a site she'd never used before, called PolitiFact. It had checked the claim, and it had a whole page for it. At the top was a little meter graphic, half-full of orange, labeled with the site's rating scale, which it called the Truth-O-Meter. This claim sat between True and False, in a zone marked Half True. Down at the bottom of the scale, past False, was a rating that made Hailey snort so hard her milk nearly came back up. "Pants on Fire."

"What?" Dad leaned over, garlic bread frozen halfway to his mouth.

"Their scale goes from True down to Pants on Fire. Like, the worst rating. This one's Half True. The site started in 2007, it says. And it rates claims, not people." She scrolled, the screen's glow bluish against the red sauce. "So the ad took something real, a few old wells that got flagged, and stretched it to sound like the whole town."

Dad chewed for a while. The kitchen clock ticked, and her brother's fork scraped his plate in slow circles. "So they didn't exactly lie," he said finally.

"They took a small true thing and made it sound huge. That's not an opinion like 'this sauce is spicy.' That's a claim with a number in it, and the number doesn't hold up. You can't check 'spicy.' You can check 'half.'"

Mom set down her ladle. "So what you're saying is, I should get a prescription for skepticism."

Hailey laughed, then stopped, because she was rereading the page. The claim had come from a political ad, and the politician was the same man whose campaign office had just called their house twice this week. The name on the screen matched the name Mom kept grumbling about.

"Mom," Hailey said slowly, turning the phone toward her. "This is the guy you were going to vote for."

Mom peered at the screen, then at Hailey, then at the little orange meter.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: A break statement stops a loop immediately, so a prime checker can quit as soon as it finds a single divisor.
story:
The basement smelled like old carpet and grape soda, and Marisol's older brother had covered one wall with posters of eccentric inventors, Tesla chief among them, glaring down over the desk where two laptops sat. Asher pulled his chair closer and cracked his knuckles.

"Okay," Marisol said. "You write it. I'm not touching the keyboard." She slid a napkin across the desk. On it, in her cramped handwriting, was the plan: ask for a number, then try dividing it by everything smaller, and print whether it was prime. Asher had exactly one reason to be here. On Friday, a kid in math class had bet him a candy bar that he couldn't explain how a computer decided such a thing, and Asher, tired of nodding along while other people understood the world, had said he could learn by Monday.

He typed while Marisol peeled electrical tape off a science-fair motor in the corner, wrapping the bare spots to insulate the wires so it wouldn't spark again. He could hear the tape ripping in little strips. The heater in the basement clanked, and somewhere behind the wall a copper conductor hummed with whatever electricity a house carried around inside it.

His first version ran. He typed 9, and the program filled the whole screen with "not prime," the same two words fifty times, scrolling and scrolling like something possessed. Asher sat back. "It works," he said, "sort of. But why so many?" He read his own loop out loud, tracing it with his finger. The answer rose up slow, the way a shape appears in fog. The loop kept going after it already knew. Every single smaller number got its own announcement. "The loop doesn't know it's done," he said. Marisol leaned over, chewing the end of a pen.

"So tell it," she said.

He wasn't sure how, so he texted his cousin, who was away at camp: MY PRIME CHECKER PRINTS NOT PRIME A MILLION TIMES HELP. The reply came as a single sentence, and Asher read it twice. "A break statement stops a loop immediately," he said aloud. Marisol wrote it on the napkin, right under the plan, and underlined "immediately" twice. So the checker could quit as soon as it found a single divisor. One divisor, one answer, done.

Asher indented a new line, typed the word, and ran it again. He entered 9 and the screen printed "not prime" exactly once, then went still and waited. He entered 7. Prime. He entered 51, feeling sneaky, and the program said "not prime" without flinching. Marisol pumped her fist and slid the candy-bar wager napkin across the desk so he could draft his reply to the kid from math class. Asher cracked his knuckles again and started typing.

"Wait," Marisol said, pointing at the screen. "What about the number one?"

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: Shirley Jackson's story The Lottery, published in The New Yorker in 1948, opens with children piling up stones, a detail that hints at how the lottery ends.
story:
Grayson slid his copy of "The Lottery" to the center of the table and tapped the first paragraph, where he had folded the corner of the page. "Read the opening again," he said. "Out loud. Trust me."

Priya, who ran the book club and had the only working thermos in the room, raised an eyebrow but picked up her own copy. "The morning of June 27th was clear and sunny, with the fresh warmth of a full-summer day; the flowers were blossoming profusely and the grass was richly green." She kept going. "Bobby Martin had already stuffed his pockets full of stones, and the other boys soon followed his example, selecting the smoothest and roundest stones."

"Stop there," Grayson said. "Yesterday I skipped right past that. Stones seemed like, I don't know, kids being kids on a nice morning." He had read the whole story that night in one sitting, and when he reached the last page he had gone back to the beginning because something about it bothered him. "But the story was in The New Yorker back in 1948, and it ends the way it ends. The stones are sitting right there in the first paragraph."

The folding table wobbled as Dev leaned forward. "So it's like a hint?"

"It's called foreshadowing," Grayson said. "The writer plants something early that points at what happens later." He felt a little shaky saying it, since until this morning he had called it "the stone thing" in his notes. "When I reread that paragraph after finishing the story, the stones weren't harmless anymore. They were the ending, hidden in plain sight on page one."

Priya set down her thermos, which she guarded like a sacred vessel, and looked almost proud, which made Grayson remember the meeting two months ago when he had shown up without reading the book and sat there barren of anything to say while everyone else argued for an hour. He had decided that night to nurture a new habit: read everything twice, once for what happens and once for how it was built.

"Okay," Dev said, flipping pages. "So what else is a hint? The black box? That's got to mean something too. The name, the color, all of it."
