"That's symbolism," Priya said slowly. "When an object stands for something bigger than itself." She frowned at her page. "Although what exactly it stands for, I'm not sure I want to say out loud yet."

Grayson pulled his chair closer and grabbed a pencil. "Then let's make a list. Every object, every detail, and we mark which ones feel like hints and which ones feel like symbols. Nobody leaves until we've argued about all of them."

Priya refilled the thermos cup and slid it across the table to him. "You want the last of the tea before we start? Because once I get going on that box, there won't be any left."

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: Japji Sahib is also recited at the Sikh Khalsa initiation ceremony, called Amrit Sanchar.
story:
Camille stood in the langar hall after morning services, a photocopied page of Gurmukhi trembling in her hand. Her grandmother had promised the whole family would come from Brampton in three weeks, and by then Camille had to know Japji Sahib by heart, every line, without the paper. She had recited it four times that morning and stumbled at the same spot every time, where the sounds doubled back on themselves like a path that loops.

Outside, her little brother Arjan flew his drone over the parking lot, its propeller catching the sun. Through the window she watched him modify the angle of the landing skids with tape, adjusting after each rough touchdown, and she thought about how he never fixed the crash, only what came after it. She had been trying to fix her mistake the same way, repeating the broken line louder, as if volume could glue the words together.

"You're grinding your teeth," said Simran, sinking onto the bench across from her. Simran was seventeen and had gone through her own ceremony last spring, though she never talked about it much. Camille wanted to ask why she'd done it so young, but that question felt like opening someone's lunchbox.

"Why does it have to be this prayer?" Camille asked instead. "Why not something shorter?" She was thinking of a conversation she wasn't supposed to have overheard, her uncle saying fourteen was too young to choose the Amrit Sanchar path, her mother saying nothing at all.

Simran turned her steel bracelet slowly around her wrist. "It's recited at the ceremony itself," she said. "The Khalsa initiation. Amrit Sanchar. You'll hear it on the day, standing right there." She said it plainly, the way you'd say the bus comes at eight, and Camille felt the ground shift a little. The prayer wasn't just a test to pass and forget. It would be in the room with her, in the moment itself, and everyone who had taken that step before her had carried the same words in their mouths.

That night Camille tried something different. Instead of attacking the broken line, she went back two lines before it and recited forward slowly, like walking a hill from the bottom instead of being dropped on the ridge. On the fourth try the difficult phrase arrived on its own, riding the rhythm of what came before it, and she understood that the mistake had never been in the line at all. It was in the approach, hidden further back, invisible until she tested it.

She called Simran, who picked up on the second ring. "I got through the whole thing," Camille said. "Twice." Through the phone came the sound of dishes being set down. "Twice," Simran repeated. "Then tomorrow you do it three times, out loud, standing up." Camille laughed, set the phone on her desk on speaker, and began again from the first line.

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: A 2001 study of school playgrounds found that when a classmate stepped in to stop bullying, the bullying stopped in more than half of the cases.
story:
Lillian sat at the kitchen table trying to look casual, which was hard with a page of notes in her lap labeled "PLAN." Across from her, eight-year-old Theo was cutting his grilled cheese into perfectly symmetrical triangles and announcing that he was an herbivore this week, "except for cheese, and also turkey on Saturdays."

"I need to practice something on you," she said. "Pretend you're Dylan Reyes."

"Theo Reyes," he said, mouth full. "That's my name now."

"Fine. Theo Reyes. Yesterday in the cafeteria, Marcus tripped carrying his tray, and Dylan laughed and called him Plates, because the tray went flying, and everyone started chanting it. Today it happened again. Tomorrow I want to do something, but if I yell at Dylan, I'll just provoke him in front of everybody and it'll get worse for Marcus. So I'm testing a different move."

Theo pushed a cheese triangle toward her as a fee. "Go ahead."

Lillian took a breath. "Hey Marcus, come sit with us, there's room." She said it flat, then tried it again, warmer, like an afterthought, like it wasn't a rescue at all. Theo chewed and considered. "The second one," he said. "The first one sounded like you felt sorry for him. Marcus hates that. He bit me at daycare once for that exact reason."

Lillian wrote "casual. warm. not sorry-sounding" on the page. Then she slid her science binder across the table and pulled out a worksheet Theo was supposed to be finishing, because Mom had put him in her charge until six. At the top of his reading sheet was a boxed fact for a question about playgrounds: In 2001, a study of school playgrounds found that when a classmate stepped in to stop bullying, the bullying stopped in more than half of the cases.

She read it twice. "Theo. Kids stepping in actually works? More than half the time?"

"That's what the box says. I have to write if it surprises me." He frowned. "It does surprise me, because Marcus is huge."

"Shhh. You're being Marcus's conscience now." Lillian tapped the worksheet with her pen. She had been assuming that stepping in meant a showdown, a speech, a confrontation that would only feed Dylan an audience. But the study didn't say the classmate fought anybody. Maybe most kids stepped in the way you'd step in anywhere: sideways, ordinary, like it was nothing. An extra tray carried. A seat offered. A chant left unjoined until it died of quiet.

The kitchen smelled like toasted butter and the lemon cleaner Mom had used on the counters, and outside somebody's sprinkler ticked against the fence in a steady rhythm, and Lillian typed a message to the group chat with one thumb while Theo watched over her shoulder like it was television.

"Marcus. Lunch tomorrow, our table, me and Priya and Sam. Bring the tray, we like the drama."

She hovered over send. Too jokey? No, jokey was right, jokey was the casual warm voice, jokey made it not a rescue. She sent it. Three dots appeared, and she held her breath through an entire symmetrical bite of Theo's cheese.

"ok," Marcus wrote. Then, "nobody's ever asked before."

Theo solemnly closed the worksheet. "Write that it surprised me," he said.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: The first food bank, St. Mary's Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, was started in 1967 by John van Hengel.
story:
Aria had never volunteered anywhere before, and the food bank took up half the library's basement, past the biography shelves and a door marked Staff Only. Her job was simple: match donation slips to boxes. By ten o'clock, the slips said there should be eleven boxes of canned vegetables, and she could only find nine.

"You lost two boxes?" Marcus worked the folding table beside her, stacking peanut butter faster than anyone. He was fourteen and wanted the supervisor to notice him so he could move up to the delivery van. "Just recount. Somebody always miscounts."

Aria counted again. Nine boxes. She checked the slips twice. Eleven written in blue ink, signed by Mr. Okafor, who had left for the bank run an hour ago. The missing boxes had existed on paper and then, somehow, evaporated between the loading dock and the basement. Nobody had taken anything out through the front, because the front was the library's circulation desk, and Priya at the desk hadn't seen a cart go by.

In the break room, while she rechecked the clipboard, Aria stopped at a framed page on the wall. The first food bank, it read, was St. Mary's Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, started in 1967 by John van Hengel. She read it twice. The words stuck with her on the walk back down, mostly because of one word: bank. A bank kept things safe and tracked them. This place tracked things with slips. If the slips were right, the boxes were somewhere, because boxes didn't just stop existing.

She tested it. If two boxes had come down on the cart, they were somewhere between the dock and the shelves. The elevator only stopped on two floors. On the main floor, past the fiction section, she found a leaning tower of boxes tucked behind the large-print mysteries, next to an eccentric old book cart with one square wheel. A man in a gray cardigan was reading the top box's label with great leisure, like he had all morning, which he apparently did.

"Those are for the food bank," Aria said.

"I know," the man said. "I volunteer Tuesdays. I set them here so I could shelve them after my shift." He blinked. "That was yesterday."

They carried the boxes down together. When she stacked them, the count came to eleven, and she showed Marcus the slip and the shelf.

"All right," Marcus said. "You were right, it wasn't a miscount." He looked at the elevator, then at her clipboard. "Next time stuff goes missing, we search the floors first. Tell Mr. Okafor it was your system."

Mr. Okafor came back from the van run, glanced at the slip, then at the full shelf, and raised an eyebrow at Aria.

"Eleven for eleven," she said.

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: With interest compounded once a year, the balance after n years equals P x (1 + r) to the power n, where r is the yearly rate as a decimal.
story:
Lydia had one hundred ninety dollars in her sock drawer and a snowboard in the mall's sporting goods window with a tag that said $549. The tag also said FINANCING AVAILABLE, in smaller letters, which Lydia suspected was the retail equivalent of a trapdoor. She had five years until she finished school and, according to the poster by the mall fountain, the new credit union kiosk was offering savings accounts at five percent. She got in line behind a man arguing about a late fee.

The teller, whose name tag said DARA, asked if Lydia needed help. Lydia slid the snowboard brochure across the counter and said she wanted to know what five percent would do to one hundred ninety dollars over five years. "Simple or compound?" Dara asked, and Lydia said, "The one that's better," because that seemed like the obvious answer. Dara handed her a calculator and said, "Compounded once a year, the balance after n years is P times 1 plus r, to the power n." Then she got pulled away by the man with the late fee, which Lydia decided was fine, since she had her own brain and a power key.

She typed 190, then multiplied by 1.05, then hit the power key with a 5, trying not to feel optimistic before she saw the number. The screen said 242.35. She stared at it. Five percent of 190 was 9.50, and five years of that was 47.50, which would make 237.50, not 242.35. She did the simple version again on paper to be sure, and it still said 237.50. The compound version was 4.85 more, which was not a fortune but was, notably, more, and it had come from nowhere she could see. She tried three years: 219.73 compound versus 218.50 simple. The gap grew every time she added a year, like something quietly accumulating behind a wall.

The man with the late fee had positioned himself to obstruct the whole kiosk, waving a statement at Dara, so Lydia worked at the end of the counter. She ran the numbers again with P as 300, just to see if the pattern belonged to her 190 dollars or to the rule itself. It belonged to the rule. Compound won by more, the longer she left it alone.

"Find out what you needed?" Dara asked, finally escaping.

"Five years of compound gets me to 242," Lydia said. "Simple gets me 237.50." She looked at the brochure. The snowboard would still cost 549. "So my actual plan is birthday money plus a summer job."

"Mathematical," Dara said, "and realistic."

Lydia folded the brochure into her back pocket and headed for the food court, already doing the arithmetic on wages and time.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: Many of the world's hot deserts lie near 30 degrees north or south of the equator, where sinking air warms up and dries out.
story:
Samantha's mother worked Saturdays at the Sunrise Travel Agency, so Samantha sat in the back with the globe, doing her science homework. Her assignment sheet said: compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs. Mrs. Alvarez had printed two graphs, one for Cairo and one for Manaus, and Samantha was supposed to write a paragraph explaining what the numbers showed. The problem was that the numbers made no sense to her. Both places were hot. Manaus got over two hundred millimeters of rain in some months. Cairo got nearly zero, all year. Same sun, same planet, and one place was a swamp and the other was sand.

She spun the globe to look for a pattern, because the paragraph was due Monday and she refused to write something random just to fill the page. The Sahara. She put her finger on it. Then the Arabian Desert, then the Kalahari, then the Australian deserts, then the Atacama. She grabbed a sticky note and marked each one, then stepped back. They were not scattered. They lined up in two bands, one north of the equator and one south of it, like belts around the planet. She measured with a ruler against the globe's stand. Roughly thirty degrees north for the Sahara, and the Kalahari sat about thirty degrees south.

"So the deserts aren't random," she said. "They're all about thirty degrees from the equator. North or south."

Her mother looked up from a brochure. "The customer who comes in at noon is booking a trip to Egypt. Ask him. He's a geography professor."

When Professor Okafor arrived, Samantha had taped her graphs to the counter beside the globe with its sticky notes. She showed him Cairo's rainfall line, flat near the bottom, next to Manaus's line, jagged and towering. "These are both hot," she said. "But the rainfall is opposite. And the deserts all line up in two belts near thirty degrees. Is that the foundation of it? Is that why Cairo's line is flat?"

He leaned over the globe, tapped the Sahara, then traced south across the equator to the Kalahari. "Many of the world's hot deserts lie near thirty degrees north or south of the equator," he said. "That's where sinking air warms up and dries out."

"Where the air dries out." Samantha wrote it fast, then crossed out her old draft. "So the flat line isn't a mistake in the data. The belt is the cause." She laid the ruler across the globe again, checking the Arabian Desert against the thirty-degree mark, and slid the sticky note two millimeters to line it up exactly.

activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
knowledge_domain: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
fact: A chapati puffs up on the heat because water in the dough turns into steam.
story:
Lucas had thirty minutes before his uncle's restaurant opened, and three things to finish at once: rice, curry, and a stack of chapatis. His uncle had left him alone in the kitchen on purpose, saying only, "Everything arrives at the table together, or nothing works." Last summer Lucas had let the rice go soft while he wrestled with the dough, and every dish had come out late and wrong. He had thought about that night all year, and he still wasn't sure whether giving up that shift had been smart or cowardly.

He started the rice first because it took longest, measuring the water the way his grandmother had shown him in her cramped flat, where the noise of the city never stopped. Then he chopped onions for the curry, keeping one ear on the bubbling pot behind him. The curry needed twenty minutes of simmering, he decided, and the chapatis only a minute or two each, so the flatbread would have to wait near the end. He wrote the order on a scrap of receipt paper, a small systematic plan: rice, curry, then bread.

His friend Dev pushed through the swinging door to drop off a delivery box and stopped dead. On the pan in front of Lucas, a flat circle of dough had suddenly ballooned, round and golden like a tiny moon. "It's alive," Dev said. "How does it do that?"

"Water in the dough turns into steam," Lucas said. "That's what puffs it up." He had learned it by accident. His first chapatis had come out flat and stiff, and he had stood there wondering what he'd missed. Then he remembered his grandmother flicking drops of water onto the dough before pressing it flat, and he had tested it, one dry circle, one wet one. The dry one stayed flat. The wet one rose.

"So you add more water and it puffs bigger?" Dev asked.

"I tried that. It just gets soggy." Lucas flipped the puffed chapati onto the wire rack and started the next one, glancing at the rice, then at the curry, checking his watch. "There's no monopoly on the answer. You have to test it."

The rice finished resting just as the curry thickened, and Lucas slid the last chapati onto the plate beside them, everything hot at the same moment. His uncle came through the door, looked at the three dishes, and said nothing, which Lucas took as the highest praise the man had ever given. Dev leaned against the counter, arms crossed. "Fine," he said, "but tomorrow I'm making one."
